323.title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what a Sikh means by seva
323.hook: the first visit: a Sikh kitchen where nobody asks who you are
323.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Buddhist means by the breath
323.howItsDone: Sikhs do seva in the gurdwara by cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, sweeping, and caring for shoes, and outside it through relief work; the langar serves a free meal to anyone who comes, seated together on the floor.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the three tracks ended: karma, bhakti, jnana. Serving, singing, asking, and all of them a doing. This week, you visit the neighbors.
screen: `KARMA · BHAKTI · JNANA — ALL A DOING.`

segments.voice: Shoes off. Head covered. Hands washed. You're in a gurdwara, a Sikh house of worship, and in the kitchen at the back someone is already handing you a plate. This week is different. Every other door on this app, Sikh, Buddhist, Muslim, Jewish, Christian, Catholic, spent its first camp teaching its own first words. Now you get to visit, one house a day. A guest has one simple rule: listen to how they say it, in their words, and don't take it home and blend it into yours.
screen: `FIRST DOOR: A GURDWARA.` → `ONE HOUSE A DAY.` → `LISTEN IN THEIR WORDS.`

segments.voice: Sit down on the floor, in a row, next to whoever's there. This kitchen is the langar, and the meal is free, to anyone, of any faith or none. Sikhs trace it to Guru Nanak, the first Guru, and to the Gurus after him. Tradition tells that the third Guru, Guru Amar Das, asked everyone who came to see him to eat in the langar first, sitting in the same rows, and that even the emperor Akbar sat on the floor and ate. Everyone at the same height. That's the first thing seva means in a Sikh home: service that erases rank. The second: it takes your whole self. Sikhs often speak of three kinds: seva with the body, like cooking, sweeping or cleaning the congregation's shoes; with the mind, like teaching or reciting; and with what you have, giving money or food. At the Golden Temple in Amritsar, volunteers cook, serve and wash dishes for whoever comes, every day, and for them the washing up is a form of worship. The third: it has no bill. In the Sukhmani, a long hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says, in effect, that the one who serves without wanting anything back is the one who reaches the Master. Seva isn't a way to earn something. For Sikhs it's a way of remembering God with your hands. You met the word seva on day fifteen; Hindus use it too. Today you heard it the way a Sikh says it, from a Sikh kitchen floor.
screen: `THE LANGAR: FREE, TO ANYONE.` · `EVERYONE AT THE SAME HEIGHT.` · `BODY, MIND AND WHAT YOU HAVE.` · `SERVICE WITH NO BILL.` · then, large: `SEVA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one time somebody fed you or served you and asked nothing back: a parent, a stranger, a nurse, a friend with soup. See their hands, and let yourself be the guest for a moment. Notice what it felt like to receive without a bill, nothing to repay, just the plate handed to you.
Seva, selfless service, as Sikhs say it: a kitchen floor where everyone eats at the same height, with your whole self, and no bill attached.

today's visit: `SEVA, AS SIKHS SAY IT.`

324.title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what a Buddhist means by the breath
324.hook: the second visit: a Buddhist hall where the only instruction is to know you're breathing
324.carry: breathe the way you're already breathing
324.tomorrow: guided visits: what the Sufis mean by remembrance
324.howItsDone: Many Buddhists, in Theravada, Zen and Tibetan communities alike, practice mindfulness of breathing, sitting quietly and knowing each breath as it comes and goes, often in a hall with a bell to begin and end.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first visit: a Sikh kitchen, and seva with no bill. Today the week's strand name, what a Buddhist means by the breath, becomes the visit.
screen: `SEVA, AS SIKHS SAY IT.`

segments.voice: A Buddhist meditation hall: a wooden floor, cushions in rows, a bell, a small statue of the Buddha at the front. You expect instructions. Relax your shoulders. Breathe in for four, hold for four. Picture a light. The teacher says none of that. She says: sit. Breathe the way you're already breathing. And know it. That's all? That's all. And people have spent their whole lives inside that one instruction. Today, the breath as the Buddhists who kept it for twenty-five centuries mean it.
screen: `A HALL, A BELL, CUSHIONS.` → `NO COUNTING, NO PICTURE.` → `JUST KNOW IT.`

segments.voice: The teaching comes from a discourse Buddhists call the Anapanasati Sutta, mindfulness of breathing, in the middle-length collection of the Buddha's talks. It opens almost like stage directions. A monk goes to the forest, or the root of a tree, or an empty hut. He sits with legs crossed and back straight, and sets mindfulness in front of him. Mindful, he breathes in. Mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in a long breath, he knows: I breathe in long. Breathing in a short breath, he knows: I breathe in short. That's the first surprise: nothing is being fixed. The long breath isn't better than the short one. The practice is knowing, not steering. The second surprise is how far it goes. The sutta lays out sixteen steps, from the length of the breath, through the whole body calming, then feelings, then the mind itself, to watching everything change and letting go. The Buddha says, in that text, that this one practice, developed, brings the four foundations of mindfulness to completion. The whole path, folded inside one breath. And why the breath? Because it's always here, and it never stays. Each breath is gone as it arrives. Buddhists call that anicca, impermanence, and the breath teaches it every four seconds without saying a word. The Buddhist door made the breath its second word, on day two. A guest just hears it their way: not a technique for power, but a place to know what's happening, right now.
screen: `MINDFUL, HE BREATHES IN.` · `KNOWING, NOT STEERING.` · `SIXTEEN STEPS, ONE BREATH.` · `EACH BREATH GONE AS IT ARRIVES.` · then, large: `THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sit, back straight, the way the text describes, and don't change the breath: when it comes in long, know it's long; when it comes in short, know it's short. When your mind wanders off, and it will, notice that too, and come back to the next breath. No counting, no picture, no goal: just a guest sitting quietly in someone else's hall.
Anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing in and out. Not controlling it; knowing it, and watching it change.
screen: `ANAPANASATI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: breathe the way you're already breathing. See you at the third house tomorrow.

325.title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what the Sufis mean by remembrance
325.hook: the third visit: a circle of people saying one line until the room goes quiet inside
325.carry: polish the heart like a mirror
325.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Jew means by Shabbat
325.howItsDone: Muslims do dhikr alone, often after the daily prayers on fingers or prayer beads; Sufi orders also gather in circles to repeat a phrase such as la ilaha illallah together, and the Mevlevi order performs a turning ceremony.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: anapanasati, the breath known, not steered, long or short. Today, a third house.
screen: `THE BREATH — KNOWING, NOT STEERING.`

segments.voice: Late on a Thursday night, in a room with carpets on the floor, twenty people sit in a circle, some old, some young, a few with their eyes closed. Someone begins a line in Arabic, softly. The circle picks it up: the same few words, again and again, a little louder, then softer, heads moving gently with the rhythm, until the words sound less like speech and more like breathing. You might have seen a clip of whirling dervishes in white skirts and tall hats. This is their family, and it's about something quieter than the spinning. Today, what the Sufis mean by remembrance.
screen: `A CIRCLE, LATE ON A THURSDAY.` → `ONE LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `WHAT THE SUFIS MEAN BY REMEMBRANCE.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is dhikr. It means remembering, and also mentioning: saying the name out loud. The Islamic door taught it as one of its first words, and it belongs to all Muslims, not only Sufis. A Muslim who whispers subhanallah or alhamdulillah after prayer is doing dhikr. The Qur'an puts it simply. In Pickthall's 1930 translation: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" And elsewhere God says, remember Me, and I will remember you. Sufis are Muslims who give their lives to that line about the heart. Sufism isn't a separate religion; it's a path inside Islam, with teachers, lineages and circles, often called orders. Many gather for dhikr together, repeating a phrase like la ilaha illallah, there is no god but God, many times over, sometimes with the breath, sometimes silently in the heart. The Mevlevi order, founded after the poet Rumi, turns remembrance into a slow turning dance. Why repeat? A Sufi would say: because the heart forgets. Not out of wickedness, just out of busyness. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported in Bukhari's collection to have said that the one who remembers his Lord and the one who doesn't are like the living and the dead. Dhikr polishes the heart, Sufis say, the way you'd polish a mirror, until it can reflect what it's facing. Muslims don't all agree about every Sufi practice; some question the music or the dancing. The heart of it is in the Qur'an itself: in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.
screen: `DHIKR: REMEMBERING, MENTIONING.` · `IN THE REMEMBRANCE, HEARTS FIND REST.` · `A CIRCLE, ONE PHRASE, AGAIN.` · `POLISHING THE MIRROR.` · then, large: `DHIKR.`

segments.voice: You're a guest in the circle, so no one expects you to say their words: just listen to the rhythm of your own breath, the way the circle listens to its line, and notice how often the mind forgets where it is and wanders off. Each time you notice, come back; that coming back is the movement a Sufi calls remembering. If you are a Muslim, you can let a phrase you already say ride quietly on the breath.
Dhikr, remembrance, the heart coming back to God, again and again.

326.title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what a Jew means by Shabbat
326.hook: the fourth visit: a Friday table, two candles, and a day that stops the week
326.carry: a day made holy by stopping
326.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Christian means by grace
326.howItsDone: Jews welcome Shabbat at sundown on Friday by lighting candles and blessing wine and bread, rest through Saturday with prayer, meals and family, and close it at nightfall with havdalah; how strictly work is set aside differs among Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and other Jews.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Sufi circle and dhikr: the heart remembering, again and again. Today, a fourth house.
screen: `DHIKR — THE HEART COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Friday, just before sunset. A kitchen that's been busy all afternoon goes suddenly still. The table has a white cloth, two braided loaves under a cover, a cup of wine or grape juice. Someone strikes a match and lights two candles, then draws her hands in toward her face and covers her eyes. Phones go face down, or away entirely, until Saturday night. From here to nightfall tomorrow, this house is keeping a day the Torah sets apart on its first page. Today, what a Jew means by Shabbat.
screen: `FRIDAY, JUST BEFORE SUNSET.` → `TWO CANDLES, TWO LOAVES.` → `WHAT A JEW MEANS BY SHABBAT.`

segments.voice: Shabbat comes from a Hebrew root that means to stop, to cease. It begins on the first page of the Torah. After six days of making the world, the text says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel pointed out that the first thing the Bible makes holy isn't a place or a person. It's a day. Later, the Ten Commandments give Shabbat twice, with two different verbs. In Exodus: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In Deuteronomy: observe it. Jewish tradition says God spoke both words at once, and some families say that's why there are two candles. Remember is the inside of the day: rest, blessing, the meal, the singing, time with the people at the table. Observe is the outside: the things you don't do. In Orthodox homes that means refraining from thirty-nine kinds of creative work the rabbis listed, from writing to kindling a fire; many Jews keep the day in other ways, with different lines, and the movements differ on how. What they share is the stop. Heschel described Shabbat as a palace built in time rather than space: a cathedral you can't visit, only enter, once a week. And the day ends the way it began, with a flame: a braided candle at Saturday nightfall, a sweet smell of spices, a blessing called havdalah, separation, and the week starts again. The Jewish door taught Shabbat as its third word. A guest hears it their way: not a day off, but a day made holy.
screen: `SHABBAT: TO STOP.` · `THE FIRST HOLY THING IS A DAY.` · `REMEMBER AND OBSERVE.` · `A PALACE IN TIME.` · then, large: `SHABBAT.`

segments.voice: Put the phone face down or out of reach, and let your hands be still, the way they'd be once a candle is lit. Let the list of unfinished things stay unfinished; it will still be there later. Breathe in: stop; breathe out: rest, a guest keeping quiet at someone else's table while they keep their day.
Shabbat, from a root meaning to stop, the seventh day made holy.

327.title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what a Christian means by grace
327.hook: the fifth visit: a song everyone knows, written by a man who didn't think he deserved to sing it
327.howItsDone: Christians speak of grace in sermons, hymns and prayers, and many say grace before meals; Catholic and Orthodox Christians receive grace especially through the sacraments, while many Protestants emphasize grace received through faith.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's house kept Shabbat: a day made holy by stopping. Today, a fifth house.
screen: `SHABBAT — A DAY MADE HOLY.`

segments.voice: A church, any church: stone or strip mall, a choir or a guitar. Sooner or later someone starts a song that long ago walked out of church and into the wider world. Amazing grace, how sweet the sound. It was published in England in 1779, by John Newton, a clergyman who had once worked in the Atlantic slave trade, and who later, publicly, turned against it. When he wrote about a grace that saved a wretch, he wasn't being modest. He meant it. Today, what a Christian means by grace.
screen: `A SONG THAT LEFT THE CHURCH.` → `JOHN NEWTON, 1779.` → `WHAT A CHRISTIAN MEANS BY GRACE.`

segments.voice: The New Testament's word is Greek: charis. It means a gift, a favor, something given freely, and it sits in a family of words about joy and thanks. So first, grace is a gift you didn't earn. Paul puts it plainly in his letter to the Ephesians. In the King James Version: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Not a wage. A gift. Second, grace finds people at their weakest, not their best. Paul writes that he begged the Lord three times to take away something he calls a thorn in the flesh, and heard this answer: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." That's why Newton could sing it. Grace, for Christians, isn't a prize for the ones who got it right. It's what meets the ones who didn't. Third, Christians differ on how grace works, and they say so. Catholic and Orthodox Christians teach that grace comes especially through the sacraments, like baptism and communion, and that a person freely cooperates with it. Many Protestants, following the Reformation, stress grace alone: salvation as God's gift, received by faith, with good works flowing from it rather than earning it. Different accounts, one word at the center. It turns up at ordinary tables too: when a family says grace before a meal, the phrase comes down from the Latin for thanks. The Christian door taught grace as its second word, and the Catholic door as its first. A guest hears it their way: love you didn't earn, and can't.
screen: `CHARIS: A GIFT, FREELY GIVEN.` · `NOT A WAGE.` · `STRENGTH MADE PERFECT IN WEAKNESS.` · `CHURCHES DIFFER ON HOW IT WORKS.` · then, large: `GRACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one good thing in your life you didn't earn, not your job, not your effort, but something given: a friend who stayed, a morning you woke up well, a person who forgave you before you asked. Let yourself receive it without explaining why you deserve it, and notice what that's like. If you pray, you can say thank you in your own way.
Charis, a gift, a favor, freely given, love that isn't earned.

328.title: The thread on your wrist
328.hook: a coworker asks about the red thread on your wrist, and the black dot on a friend's baby
328.carry: someone was looking out for you
328.howItsDone: Many priests tie a red and yellow kalava thread on the wrist at the end of a puja; many families put a small dot of kajal on a baby against nazar, the evil eye, and some shops hang a lemon and seven green chilies by the door.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's house spoke of grace, charis. Your line was love you didn't earn. Today the visits turn around: for two days, the questions neighbors ask about your house. Day three hundred twenty-eight.
screen: `CHARIS — LOVE YOU DIDN'T EARN.`

segments.voice: A coworker notices it while you're both waiting for coffee: a red and yellow thread, a little faded, tied around your wrist. Is that a friendship bracelet? Not quite. A priest tied it at a puja weeks ago, and you haven't had the heart to cut it off. Then she mentions her friend's new baby, who had a black smudge on her cheek at the naming party, and she wasn't sure whether to say something. Two questions. One answer underneath both.
screen: `A RED AND YELLOW THREAD.` → `A BLACK SMUDGE ON A BABY.` → `ONE ANSWER UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: The thread is called kalava, or mauli, and many priests call it a raksha sutra, a protection thread. It's usually red and yellow cotton, tied on the wrist at the end of a puja while a short verse is said. In many families it goes on the right wrist for men and the left for married women, though customs differ. You wear it until it falls off, or until the next puja. It's a cousin of the rakhi from day eighty-four, but anyone can receive it, from anyone who blesses. The black smudge is kajal, the soft black of eyeliner, put on a baby's cheek or forehead or behind the ear. Its job is to ward off nazar, the evil eye. Nazar simply means a look. The worry is that too much admiration, even loving admiration, can bring harm to something new and beautiful. So a small flaw is added on purpose. The same idea hangs on shop doors as a lemon and seven green chilies on a string. An honest note. These are folk customs, loved and widely kept across South Asia, by Hindus and by neighbors of other faiths too, and they aren't commands from the old scriptures. Some families take them seriously, some keep them with a smile, some skip them. All of those are Hindu homes. But look underneath. A thread on a wrist and a dot on a cheek say the same thing: someone was looking out for you. So here's a short, true answer for the coffee line. It's a blessing for protection. Someone tied it on me with love.
screen: `KALAVA — A PROTECTION THREAD.` · `KAJAL AGAINST NAZAR, THE EVIL EYE.` · `FOLK CUSTOM, NOT SCRIPTURE.` · `SOMEONE WAS LOOKING OUT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Rest your attention on your wrist, as if a thread were tied there, and think of someone who has looked out for you, out loud or quietly: tied a thread, said a prayer, worried at the door until you got home. Let the feeling sit on your skin for a few breaths. If you pray, you can send the blessing back to them.
Nazar. A look: the evil eye that families ward off with a black dot, a thread, or a lemon and seven chilies. Today's word.
screen: `NAZAR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: someone was looking out for you. That's the whole thread. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

329.title: When someone is unkind
329.hook: a stranger on a late train tells a woman born in her city that she doesn't belong; the raised hand on the murtis
329.carry: your worth isn't up for a vote
329.tomorrow: The first mountain, from the top
329.howItsDone: Many murtis of Ganesha, Durga, Vishnu and Shiva show one hand raised, palm out, in the abhaya mudra, the gesture of 'do not fear'.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, nazar: a thread on a wrist and a dot on a cheek. Your line was someone was looking out for you. Today, the harder question: when the look isn't kind. Day three hundred twenty-nine.
screen: `SOMEONE WAS LOOKING OUT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: She was born in this city. She went to school here, works here, loves it. One evening on a late train, a stranger tells her she doesn't really belong here, and throws in a slur meant for a religion that isn't even hers. Then he gets off at the next stop. She sits there shaking, the train still moving, everyone looking at their phones. A lot of people know a version of that night. This week has been about neighbors. Today, the hard part: when a neighbor isn't kind.
screen: `A LATE TRAIN.` → `YOU DON'T BELONG HERE.` → `WHEN A NEIGHBOR ISN'T KIND.`

segments.voice: Start with something you can see on almost any shrine. Look at Ganesha, or Durga, or Vishnu. One hand is often raised, palm out, fingers up. That's the abhaya mudra. Abhaya means no fear. The gesture says: don't be afraid. Here's what the tradition puts in that hand. First, your worth isn't up for a vote. You met the atman on day ten: someone is in there. In the Gita, Krishna says weapons can't cut it and fire can't burn it. A stranger's words can shake you. They can't reach that. Second, dignity, not hate. Ahimsa, from day seventeen, means not harming, and that includes not answering cruelty with more cruelty. It never means staying silent or staying unsafe. Move away. Tell someone. Report it. Ask for help. Third, pride without a ladder. You can love your festivals, your food, your temples, your grandmother's songs, without claiming anyone else's are lower. One truth, many names asks exactly that. And fourth, you're not alone. Lean on your people. If you're ever in danger, call local emergency services. If a night like that leaves you somewhere dark, in the US you can call or text 988, any hour, and talk to someone; elsewhere, local emergency help is there too. This week you visited five other houses and heard each in its own words. The bow from day four still holds, even when someone doesn't bow back: the light in me sees the light in you.
screen: `ABHAYA — DON'T BE AFRAID.` · `YOUR WORTH ISN'T UP FOR A VOTE.` · `DIGNITY, NOT HATE.` · `YOU'RE NOT ALONE.`

segments.voice: If you like, lift your right hand, palm out, the way the murtis do, and name a moment someone made you feel small, without reliving it. Breathe in slowly, and on the out-breath let the hand say what it says: don't be afraid. If you pray, you can ask for courage; if you don't, let the steady breath be the answer. Lower your hand when you're ready.
Abhaya mudra. The raised open palm on so many murtis: no fear, don't be afraid. Today's word.
screen: `ABHAYA MUDRA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: your worth isn't up for a vote. Nobody on a train gets to decide it. See you tomorrow.
